lines.text: In nineteen twenty-five, one man actually sold the Eiffel Tower.
The buyer handed over a fortune.
But there was one enormous problem.
The seller didn't own it.
And somehow, he got away with it.
To understand how this happened, we need to go back to Paris in the nineteen-twenties.
The Eiffel Tower was already famous, but not everyone loved it.
Maintaining the enormous iron structure was expensive.
Then a man named Victor Lustig arrived in Paris.
He was an experienced con artist, known for his expensive suits and convincing manners.
When he read about the tower's maintenance problems, he saw an opportunity.
Lustig pretended to be a senior French government official.
He arranged a private meeting with scrap-metal businessmen at the luxurious Hôtel de Crillon.
They believed they were about to hear an important government announcement.
He told them the government had decided to dismantle the Eiffel Tower and sell its metal.
The businessmen were stunned.
One of the world's most famous landmarks, about to be taken apart?
But Lustig insisted the decision was confidential.
Among them was André Poisson, a businessman eager to establish himself in Paris.
He believed buying the tower's metal could be a huge opportunity.
And Lustig's convincing performance made the impossible sound real.
Eventually, Poisson paid Lustig a substantial sum, believing he had secured the deal.
He thought he had purchased thousands of tons of iron.
Lustig took the money and disappeared from Paris.
Only afterward did Poisson discover the truth.
The French government had never agreed to sell the tower.
The entire deal was a fraud.
But Poisson was so embarrassed that he reportedly never went to the police.
And here's the unbelievable part.
Lustig later returned to Paris and tried to sell the Eiffel Tower again.
This time, the plan failed.
Suspecting that the authorities had been alerted, he left France.
Lustig continued committing fraud in America.
But in nineteen thirty-five, he was arrested.
He was eventually sentenced to twenty years in prison for other crimes.
The man who had sold a famous landmark was finally caught.
And almost a century later, the Eiffel Tower is still standing.
Imagine discovering you'd paid for a landmark that was never yours.
Would you have believed him?
